hero.headline: Fight to save rare deep-sea coral reef off Fort Pierce heads to final federal decision
hero.body:
Dozens of community members gathered at Blake Library in Martin County after a federally appointed council voted to roll back longstanding protections for the Oculina Bank, a rare deep-water coral reef located just off the coast of Fort Pierce. The reef, found nowhere else on Earth, thrives in deep, dark waters hundreds of feet below the surface and is home to more than 2,000 marine species.

Two proposals would reopen parts of the reef to shrimp trawling, even though scientists say trawling destroyed as much as 90% of the reef before federal protections were put in place decades ago. Dr. Grant Gilmore, a scientist who previously dived the reef, warned that removing the habitat and food source the coral provides would eliminate the fish that depend on it. Mark Perry, executive director of the Florida Oceanographic Society, and other scientists urged the public to help save the reef, noting that corals worldwide are in trouble.

The proposals followed a Trump executive order issued in April 2025 that tasked eight regional councils nationwide to find ways to reinvigorate fishing industries. Bob Zales, executive director of the Southeastern Fishing Association and a generational shrimper, told reporters he believes reopening shrimping access to the Oculina Bank is essential for the struggling rock shrimp industry. Council data shows the rock shrimp industry has plummeted from over 700 trips per year in the mid-1990s to under 100 since 2010, with the number of active rock shrimpers dropping from 144 in 1996 to less than 30, with just 12 active boats in 2018.

Zales attributes the decline to high costs, competition from imported shrimp and closures of previously open fishing areas. But scientists warned reopening the reef could irreparably damage what little remains of the rare ecosystem. The federal agency is now preparing a final ruling on the fate of the Oculina Bank as the debate continues between conservation and industry interests.

cards.headline: Florida voters to decide on massive property tax cut this November
cards.teaser: Florida lawmakers passed a proposal Tuesday that would increase the homestead exemption from $50,000 to $250,000 over two years, but the measure needs approval from 60% of voters in November.
cards.body:
Florida lawmakers on Tuesday passed a property tax cut proposal that would increase the homestead exemption from $50,000 to $250,000 over two years, with inflation adjustments beginning in 2029. The bill needs approval from 60% of voters in November to take effect. The measure would also lower assessment caps on non-homesteaded properties from 10% to 5%.

Experts are divided on what the ripple effects could be for local governments and residents. Real estate attorney Steve Wallace, based in Boynton Beach, raised the possibility of new fees tied to local services, suggesting there could be non-ad valorem taxes assigned to the sheriff's office or fire rescue, or increased fees because those are the only other ways county or local governments can derive revenue. CPA Paul Miller suggested businesses could end up carrying more of the financial burden to offset lost revenue through annual fees.

Municipal attorney Raul Gastesi offered a different perspective, suggesting the measure could actually push home prices higher because home buyers would have more money at their disposal. However, realtor Danielle Blake was skeptical, pointing to interest rates as a more significant barrier to sales than property taxes alone. All four experts acknowledged there are significant unknowns about how counties, municipalities and markets might respond to decreasing property tax revenue. If the ballot measure passes, lawmakers would need to return to Tallahassee to work out the specifics in a bill to implement the changes.

cards.headline: Three arrested in Operation Hammer Time theft ring that hit Stuart, Fort Pierce, Jupiter hardware stores
cards.teaser: A retail theft operation targeted at least 40 hardware stores across 13 counties, including locations in Stuart, Fort Pierce, and Jupiter, resulting in roughly $500,000 in stolen property and damage.
cards.body:
The Martin County Sheriff's Office announced arrests in a retail theft ring dubbed Operation Hammer Time that targeted hardware stores across Martin, Palm Beach, and St. Lucie counties. Johnny Batista, 19, Roberto Hernandez-Castro, 39, and Roberto Aldana-Ferrera, 31, were all involved in a series of burglaries from December 2025 to April 2026. Major Ruben Romero said at least 40 stores across 13 counties were burglarized, with stolen goods taken back to Miami-Dade County, where the suspects lived, to be sold.

According to Martin County Sheriff's Office affidavits, hardware stores in Stuart, Lake Worth, Delray Beach, Boynton Beach, West Palm Beach, Fort Pierce, and Jupiter were targeted, along with stores in Broward County. The crews would use a sledgehammer or other blunt object to smash the glass and often complete the thefts within minutes, before police arrived or alarms were triggered. Roughly $500,000 worth of property was stolen, in addition to damage to stores.

Aldana-Ferrera is in custody in Georgia, Batista was arrested in February for a vehicle theft and is in Martin County Jail, and Hernandez-Castro has a warrant out for his arrest. A fourth suspect, Maikell Fleitas, is deceased. The suspects are facing charges of racketeering, burglary over $1,000 in damage while masked, burglary of an occupied structure, and burglary of an unoccupied structure. Major Romero noted the thefts contribute to inflation and make it harder for working residents to afford tools.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie woman sentenced to 3 years in prison for running illegal med spa out of backyard shed
cards.teaser: Rosa Mena, 50, of Port St.
cards.body:
Rosa Mena, 50, of Port St. Lucie has been sentenced to three years in prison and five years of probation after operating an unlicensed medical spa out of a shed in her backyard. The sentencing follows her arrest for performing cosmetic procedures without proper medical credentials at her business, Miracle Hand and Spa, located on the 5000 block of Northwest Coosa Drive.

Mena came to the attention of authorities in May 2025 when a victim reported experiencing partial facial paralysis after receiving 62 units of Botox injections at the makeshift facility. The victim, who had been referred to the business by coworkers, paid $325 for the services. When confronted about the paralysis, Mena refunded the money and offered another injection of vitamins to reverse the issues. The victim later requested Mena's medical license, and Mena provided an altered phlebotomy certificate that had actually expired in February 2024. Mena also falsely claimed to be a doctor from the Dominican Republic.

A multi-agency investigation involving Port St. Lucie Police, PSL Code Enforcement, the PSL Building Department, PSL Business Tax, and the Florida Department of Health led to a search warrant at Mena's residence. Detectives found medical beds, fat sculpting machines, laser hair removal equipment, laser liposuction machines, and injection devices for fillers and Botox inside the backyard shed.

Mena was charged with three counts of aggravated battery causing bodily harm, three counts of practicing medicine without an active license, one count of fraud to obtain property $300 or more, one count of fraud to obtain property under $20,000, and one count of use of a two-way communication device to facilitate a felony. The case serves as a reminder for Port St. Lucie residents to verify medical credentials before receiving cosmetic procedures.

cards.headline: Martin County Sheriff breaks up multi-county hardware store theft ring in Operation Hammer Time
cards.body:
The Martin County Sheriff's Office announced the arrest of three men involved in a retail theft ring that targeted more than 40 hardware stores across 13 counties between December 2025 and April 2026. Major Ruben Romero identified the suspects as Johnny Batista, 19, Roberto Hernandez-Castro, 39, and Roberto Aldana-Ferrera, 31. The crew stole roughly $500,000 worth of property and caused extensive damage to stores across Martin, Palm Beach and St. Lucie counties, according to Romero.

The suspects hit hardware stores in Stuart, Lake Worth, Delray Beach, Boynton Beach, West Palm Beach, Fort Pierce and Jupiter, as well as stores in Broward County. Investigators say the crews used sledgehammers or other blunt objects to smash glass and often completed the thefts within minutes, before police arrived or alarms were triggered. The stolen goods were taken back to Miami-Dade County, where the suspects lived, to be sold.

Batista was arrested in February for a vehicle theft and remains in Martin County Jail. Aldana-Ferrera is in custody in Georgia, while Hernandez-Castro has a warrant out for his arrest. A fourth suspect, Maikell Fleitas, is deceased. Romero connected Batista to the first known theft at Sewell Hardware in Stuart in December 2025, though investigators believe burglaries happened earlier.

The suspects face charges including racketeering, burglary over $1,000 in damage while masked, burglary of an occupied structure, and burglary of an unoccupied structure. Romero said the thefts have a broader impact on the community. "There's already inflation that we notice severely in our state, and the more they steal, the more damage they cause, the more expensive things are. People can't go to work because they can't afford the tools." Investigators are still looking for one other suspect.

cards.headline: Black bear spotted swimming through Port St. Lucie neighborhood
cards.teaser: Port St. Lucie police shared rare video footage of a black bear swimming through a waterway in the Town Park community before exiting the water and running toward nearby homes.
cards.body:
Port St. Lucie police shared rare video footage Tuesday of a black bear swimming through a waterway in the Town Park community before exiting the water and running toward nearby homes, marking an unusual wildlife sighting along the Treasure Coast. The video, posted on the Port St. Lucie Police Department's Facebook page, shows the large black bear navigating through residential waters in what officials described as seasonal behavior for Florida's black bear population.

The Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission Bear Management Program said they are monitoring the bear. If it does not move from the area on its own, bear biologists may set a trap to try and capture and relocate it. Port St. Lucie police stated that as Florida's black bears become more active this time of year in search of food, occasional sightings in residential neighborhoods can occur. According to the FWC, bear sightings remain rare throughout most of the Treasure Coast and Palm Beach County regions, making Tuesday's encounter particularly noteworthy for local residents.

Wildlife officials recommend maintaining significant distance if residents spot a bear, never approaching the animal, and avoiding any attempts to feed it. Port St. Lucie police advise residents to keep children and pets away from bears and secure potential food sources including garbage, pet food, and bird seed around their properties. During unexpected bear encounters, officials stress remaining calm and avoiding running. Instead, residents should slowly back away while keeping the bear visible, speak in calm, firm tones, and ensure the animal has a clear escape route.

cards.headline: St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office swears in 12 Make-A-Wish kids as junior deputies
cards.teaser: Twelve kids from the Make-A-Wish Foundation were sworn in as junior deputies by St. Lucie County Sheriff Richard Del Toro, including twin siblings who went through a bone marrow transplant together.
cards.body:
Twelve kids from the Make-A-Wish Foundation were sworn in as junior deputies by St. Lucie County Sheriff Richard Del Toro on Wednesday. Sheriff Del Toro called it one of the greatest days in his career. The junior deputies received badges, toured the sheriff's office, and saw the helicopter, SWAT team, and K-9 demonstrations.

Among the newest junior deputies were twins Mia and Daryl. In 2023, Mia was diagnosed with aplastic anemia, a blood disorder, and needed a bone marrow transplant. Her twin brother Daryl donated his bone marrow to save his sister's life. Their mother, Melissa Nyack, said her son was in a wheelchair and endured a lot of pain during the process. Mia said she was scared, but her brother made her feel safe.

Another junior deputy, Tobias, was diagnosed with B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia in 2022. His mother, Charity Deleon, said things that don't normally happen to a child happened to him. She said they even lost him at one point, and medical staff were able to bring him back, and he miraculously recovered. Deleon thanked the sheriff's office for making the time and energy to welcome the children into the community and remind them that they're important. Sheriff Del Toro said the heroes left an imprint on the department, saying the kids made their wish come true.

cards.body:

Built in 1909 along South Indian River Drive, the home is listed on the National Register of Historic Places and has served a variety of roles over the decades. Co-owner Georgette Angelos said Fort Pierce is eclectic, artistic, and has deep, beautiful history. The goal behind the historic doors is to make guests feel at home while honoring the building's legacy. Originally built by an engineer for Henry Flagler's Florida East Coast Railway, who later became St. Lucie County's third sheriff, the Boston House remains closely tied to the region's early development. During renovations, the owners intentionally preserved historic details, including low original ceilings and Florida-themed law books that nod to the home's past.

General manager Scott Laird said the revival of the property reflects broader momentum downtown. He noted that Fort Pierce has had a reputation, but the city has done a great job bringing new life to the downtown area. Each room in the Boston House offers a distinct experience rooted in local history, blending preservation with a modern dining atmosphere. Laird said it's important to hold onto the greatness in the area and shine a spotlight on it. The Boston House now stands as both a historic landmark and a renewed gathering place serving up a new chapter for downtown Fort Pierce.

Delays in restaurant openings have become common in Florida, often due to permitting processes, construction challenges, or staffing issues. The opening this week marks the end of the wait for customers eager to try the new establishment.

cards.headline: Two Raising Cane's chicken restaurants coming to Florida locations
cards.teaser: Raising Cane's is opening two new restaurants in Florida as part of the chain's expansion across the United States.
cards.body:
Raising Cane's chicken finger restaurants are expanding in Florida with two new locations planned for the state. The Louisiana-based chain is part of a broader expansion effort that includes openings across the United States.

Raising Cane's has developed a loyal following for its focused menu of chicken fingers, fries, coleslaw, and signature sauce. The chain has been growing rapidly in Florida, where it competes with other fast-casual chicken restaurants for market share.

The two Florida locations will add to the company's presence in the state. While the specific Treasure Coast impact depends on where the restaurants open, the expansion reflects the continued growth of the fast-casual dining sector across Florida communities.

cards.headline: Indian River County restaurant earns perfect score while another fails inspection
cards.teaser: Health inspections in Indian River County produced contrasting results, with one restaurant scoring perfectly and another failing its inspection.
cards.body:
A restaurant in Indian River County received a perfect score during recent health inspections, while another establishment failed its inspection. The contrasting results highlight the range of food safety practices across dining establishments in the county.

Health inspections are conducted regularly by the Florida Department of Business and Professional Regulation to ensure restaurants maintain proper food safety standards. Inspectors check for issues including proper food temperatures, cleanliness, and employee hygiene practices.

Restaurants that fail inspections must address the violations and undergo follow-up inspections to verify compliance. Indian River County residents can access inspection reports online to review the safety records of restaurants before dining out, helping them make informed choices about where to eat.

hero.headline: Martin County schools police chief arrested for DUI
hero.body:
The police chief for Martin County schools was arrested on DUI charges Wednesday evening, according to reports from local law enforcement.

The arrest of the district's top school safety official raises questions about leadership within the Martin County School District's police department. School police chiefs oversee security operations across all campuses in the district, including Stuart, Jensen Beach, Palm City, and Hobe Sound area schools.

The Martin County School District employs its own police force separate from the Martin County Sheriff's Office to provide security at elementary, middle, and high schools throughout the county. The department is responsible for protecting students and staff across dozens of campuses.

The arrest comes during a time when school safety remains a priority for parents and administrators across Florida. The school district has not yet announced whether the police chief will remain in his position or what interim leadership arrangements might be put in place.

cards.headline: Florida legislature approves expanded homestead tax exemption for voters to decide
cards.teaser: The state legislature has approved putting a constitutional amendment on the ballot that would expand Florida's homestead property tax exemption, a move that could affect homeowners across Martin, St. Lucie, and Indian River counties.
cards.body:
Florida lawmakers have passed legislation to place a constitutional amendment before voters that would expand the state's homestead property tax exemption. The measure will appear on an upcoming ballot for Florida residents to decide.

The homestead exemption currently provides property tax relief to Florida homeowners on their primary residences. An expansion would reduce the taxable value of homes, potentially lowering annual tax bills for property owners across the Treasure Coast and throughout the state.

If approved by voters, the expanded exemption could have significant implications for local government budgets in Martin, St. Lucie, and Indian River counties. Property taxes fund essential services including schools, law enforcement, fire rescue, road maintenance, and other county and municipal operations. Local governments may need to adjust their revenue planning depending on how voters respond to the amendment.

cards.headline: Stuart remains without connection between Breeze Airways and Brightline rail service
cards.teaser: A Florida city has secured coordination between Breeze Airways and Brightline rail service, but Stuart is not that city, according to a recent opinion piece addressing transportation gaps on the Treasure Coast.
cards.body:
While some Florida communities have managed to link air and rail transportation options, Stuart continues to operate without a coordinated connection between Breeze Airways flights and Brightline passenger rail service. The observation highlights ongoing transportation challenges for Treasure Coast residents.

Brightline's passenger rail line runs through Martin County with a station in Stuart, providing connections to South Florida and eventually to Orlando. Breeze Airways operates from various Florida airports, but the lack of seamless coordination between the two services means travelers must arrange their own connections.

The disconnect affects business travelers and tourists who might otherwise find Stuart and the broader Treasure Coast more accessible. Other Florida cities that have established better coordination between air and rail services may have an advantage in attracting visitors and supporting economic development. For Stuart residents, the gap means additional planning is required when trips involve both air and rail travel.

cards.headline: Fort Myers Beach candidates file for November town council race
cards.teaser: Three candidates have filed to run for Fort Myers Beach Town Council seats in the November election, with qualifying week approaching.
cards.body:
Fort Myers Beach Councilmember Rebecca Link, Local Planning Agency member Edward Schoonover, and Protect FMB President Tom Brady have submitted paperwork to run for Town Council seats in the November election. Link is seeking re-election after winning her seat last November.

The Lee County Supervisor of Elections office has set the official qualifying period from noon on June 8 through June 12. Candidates must submit their paperwork and pay election fees during that window to officially qualify for the ballot. Pre-qualifying began this past week, allowing candidates to submit materials early.

The town council election comes as Fort Myers Beach continues recovery and rebuilding efforts. The council makes decisions on development, zoning, budget priorities, and other matters affecting the barrier island community. Voters will head to the polls in November to decide which candidates will represent them on the council.

cards.headline: Southwest Florida baseball all-area team and player of the year announced
cards.teaser: The News-Press has named its 2026 Southwest Florida Baseball All-Area team and Player of the Year, recognizing top high school baseball talent from the region.
cards.body:
High school baseball players from across Southwest Florida have been recognized on the 2026 All-Area team, with one standout named Player of the Year. The annual honors celebrate the best baseball talent from the spring season.

The all-area selections represent the culmination of the high school baseball season, recognizing players who demonstrated exceptional skill, leadership, and performance on the field. Coaches, statistics, and game performance all factor into the selection process.

While the all-area team focuses on Southwest Florida programs, the recognition highlights the depth of baseball talent in the region. Many of these players will go on to compete at the college level, with some potentially reaching professional baseball. The honors also reflect the strength of high school athletic programs and coaching across the area.

cards.headline: Florida property tax changes could affect funding for children's programs
cards.teaser: Proposed property tax changes in Florida could impact funding for programs serving children, raising concerns about the state's safety net services.
cards.body:
A property tax overhaul being considered in Florida has raised concerns about potential impacts on funding for children's services and safety net programs. The changes could affect how local governments and agencies fund programs that serve vulnerable children across the state.

Property taxes in Florida fund a wide range of local services, including child welfare programs, youth services, after-school programs, and other initiatives designed to support children and families. Any significant changes to property tax structures could require local governments to make difficult budgeting decisions.

For Treasure Coast communities, the potential funding implications could affect programs in Martin, St. Lucie, and Indian River counties. Local officials and advocates who work with children and families are watching the property tax discussions closely to understand how any changes might impact services that residents depend on. The debate reflects broader tensions in Florida between tax relief for property owners and maintaining funding for essential services.

cards.headline: Stuart home listed for sale on SE Mentmore Lane
cards.teaser: A residential property at 3905 SE Mentmore Lane in Stuart has been listed for sale, joining the local real estate market.
cards.body:
A home located at 3905 SE Mentmore Lane in Stuart has been listed on the real estate market. The property listing appeared on Realtor.com this week.

SE Mentmore Lane is in a residential area of Stuart in Martin County. The listing reflects ongoing real estate activity in the Treasure Coast housing market, where inventory and buyer demand continue to shape the local economy.

The Stuart area real estate market serves a mix of year-round residents, retirees, and seasonal visitors drawn to the community's waterfront location and small-town character. Home sales and property values remain important indicators of economic health for Martin County and the broader Treasure Coast region.

hero.headline: Treasure Coast Readers Asked to Vote for All-Time Best Girls Basketball Player
hero.body:
Local sports fans across Martin, St. Lucie, and Indian River counties are being asked to cast their votes for the Treasure Coast's all-time best girls basketball player. The voting initiative celebrates the rich history of girls basketball in the region and recognizes the outstanding athletes who have competed for area high schools over the years.

The voting process gives residents a chance to weigh in on which local player made the greatest impact on the court during their high school career. Girls basketball has a strong tradition on the Treasure Coast, with teams from Stuart, Fort Pierce, Port St. Lucie, Vero Beach, and other communities regularly competing at high levels.

The selection of an all-time best player reflects both individual achievement and the lasting impression these athletes made on their schools and communities. Many former Treasure Coast girls basketball players have gone on to compete at the college level and beyond, building on foundations established in local gyms.

Voting allows longtime fans and newer residents alike to learn about the history of girls basketball across the three counties. The recognition honors the dedication and skill of athletes who represented their schools and brought pride to their communities through their performances on the basketball court.

cards.headline: St. Lucie Mets Host Clearwater Threshers for Six-Game Series at Clover Park
cards.teaser: The St. Lucie Mets welcome the Clearwater Threshers to Port St. Lucie for a six-day series at Clover Park, bringing minor league baseball action to the Treasure Coast.
cards.body:
Baseball fans in Port St. Lucie have six straight days of minor league action ahead as the St. Lucie Mets take on the Clearwater Threshers at Clover Park. The extended series gives local fans multiple opportunities to catch games at the home ballpark.

Clover Park serves as the spring training facility for the New York Mets and is the home field for the St. Lucie Mets during the minor league season. The venue provides an accessible and family-friendly option for Treasure Coast residents looking to enjoy live baseball without traveling to major league stadiums.

The series format allows the teams to play multiple games over nearly a week, typical of minor league scheduling. Fans can watch developing talent as players work their way through the New York Mets farm system, with many eventually advancing to higher levels of professional baseball.

cards.headline: Florida High School Football Open Division Playoff Format Announced by FHSAA
cards.teaser: The Florida High School Athletic Association has released the playoff format for the new Open Division, affecting how top high school football teams across the state will compete for championships.
cards.body:
High school football programs across Florida now have clarity on how the new Open Division playoff system will work, following the release of the format by the Florida High School Athletic Association. The Open Division represents a significant change to the state's high school football postseason structure.

The new format will affect how teams from the Treasure Coast and throughout the state compete for football championships. High schools in Martin, St. Lucie, and Indian River counties that field competitive football programs will need to understand the new playoff criteria and structure as they prepare for upcoming seasons.

The FHSAA's decision to create an Open Division reflects ongoing discussions about how to organize playoff competition among schools of varying enrollment sizes and competitive levels. The change aims to create more balanced postseason matchups while still providing championship opportunities for programs across different classifications.

cards.headline: Coconut Creek Football Program Earning Greater Recruiting Recognition
cards.teaser: The Coconut Creek High School football program is gaining increased attention in recruiting circles, with offensive and defensive linemen now drawing the same level of scrutiny traditionally reserved for skill position players.
cards.body:
Recruiting dynamics in South Florida high school football continue to evolve, with programs like Coconut Creek High School now receiving recognition that reflects changing priorities among college scouts and recruiters. The attention paid to linemen has grown substantially, matching the focus historically given to quarterbacks, running backs, and receivers.

Football recruiting has shifted in recent years as college programs place greater emphasis on identifying talented linemen earlier in the process. The days when only skill position players competed in high-profile 7-on-7 events while linemen received less attention have given way to more comprehensive evaluation of all positions.

Coconut Creek's rising profile in recruiting demonstrates how programs can build reputations by developing talent across all position groups. The increased recognition benefits both the school's football program and individual players seeking college opportunities, reflecting the program's commitment to developing well-rounded teams rather than relying solely on star skill players.

cards.headline: Minor League Baseball Teams Across Nation Planning PLAY BALL Weekend Events
cards.teaser: Minor league baseball clubs nationwide, including teams in Florida, are preparing special activities and promotions for PLAY BALL Weekend, celebrating youth baseball and softball participation.
cards.body:
Minor league baseball organizations across the country are gearing up for PLAY BALL Weekend, an initiative designed to promote youth participation in baseball and softball. Teams are planning special events, activities, and promotions to encourage young people to get involved in the sports.

The PLAY BALL Weekend concept brings together professional baseball at the minor league level with grassroots efforts to introduce children to the game. Participating teams typically offer youth clinics, special ticket promotions for families, and on-field opportunities for young players to experience professional ballparks.

For Treasure Coast families interested in baseball and softball, the initiative represents an opportunity to connect with the sport at the minor league level. Events like these help build connections between professional teams and local communities while encouraging physical activity and teamwork among young athletes.

cards.headline: Southwest Florida Baseball Names All-Area Team and Player of the Year
cards.teaser: High school baseball standouts from Southwest Florida have been recognized with selections to the all-area team, with one player earning top honors as Player of the Year.
cards.body:
The Southwest Florida baseball community has announced its all-area team selections, recognizing the top high school players from the region's spring season. One player received the distinction of being named Player of the Year, the highest individual honor for the area.

All-area team selections celebrate the achievements of high school baseball players who excelled during the season. The recognition considers both statistics and overall impact on their teams' success, highlighting players who stood out among their peers across multiple schools.

These honors carry significance for players as they conclude their high school careers or prepare for senior seasons. Being named to an all-area team provides recognition of hard work and talent, and for some players, can help attract attention from college coaches and scouts evaluating prospects for the next level of competition.

cards.headline: Daytona Tortugas Complete First Two Months of Minor League Season
cards.teaser: The Daytona Tortugas have wrapped up the first two months of their minor league baseball season, with a review of team performance and notable player developments.
cards.body:
The Daytona Tortugas have reached the two-month mark of their minor league season, providing an opportunity to assess the team's performance and individual player progress. The review covers how the team has fared through the early portion of the schedule and highlights standout performances.

Minor league baseball teams like the Tortugas serve as developmental platforms for major league organizations, in this case working within a parent club's farm system. The first two months of any season reveal which players are advancing their skills and which may be ready for promotion to higher levels of competition.

The Tortugas play in Daytona Beach, making them one of the closest minor league teams to Treasure Coast residents. Many local baseball fans travel to Daytona for affordable family entertainment and to watch prospects who may eventually reach the major leagues, making the team's progress of regional interest.

hero.headline: Treasure Coast Fourth of July guide released for America's 250th birthday celebrations
hero.body:
Treasure Coast residents can begin planning their Independence Day celebrations with a comprehensive guide to Fourth of July events across Martin, St. Lucie, and Indian River counties. This year marks America's 250th birthday, and communities throughout the region are preparing special celebrations to commemorate the historic milestone.

The guide provides information on fireworks displays, parades, and community gatherings scheduled for July 4 across the three-county area. Residents can use the resource to find family-friendly activities close to home, from beachfront celebrations to traditional town square events.

The 250th anniversary of American independence, known as the semiquincentennial, is expected to draw larger crowds than usual to local Fourth of July events. Communities across the Treasure Coast have been preparing enhanced programming to mark the historic occasion.

Families planning their holiday weekend can access the complete guide through Treasure Coast News to find event times, locations, and parking information for celebrations in their area. The guide covers events from Sebastian and Vero Beach in Indian River County through Fort Pierce and Port St. Lucie in St. Lucie County, and Stuart, Jensen Beach, and other Martin County communities.

cards.headline: 80-mile ocean paddle crossing to arrive at Lake Worth Beach June 13 to benefit cystic fibrosis families
cards.teaser: More than 100 paddlers will cross the Atlantic Ocean from Bimini to Lake Worth Beach in a 12 to 16-hour endurance event raising money for cystic fibrosis families.
cards.body:
More than 100 paddlers will launch from Bimini, Bahamas, at midnight on June 13 and paddle 80 miles across the open Atlantic Ocean before arriving at Lake Worth Beach. The annual Crossing for Cystic Fibrosis expects participants to complete the crossing in 12 to 16 hours, with spectators invited to Lake Worth Beach for a daylong celebration marking their arrival.

The endurance event benefits the Pipers Angels Foundation, established by event founder Travis Suit in honor of his daughter Piper, who was diagnosed with cystic fibrosis at age 4. Participants must raise at least $2,000 for the cause, with crew and virtual participants required to raise $500. Final contributions are due July 31. Cystic fibrosis is a life-shortening genetic condition that affects the lungs and digestive system.

The crossing is part of a four-day schedule beginning June 10 with arrivals and a poolside social at Bimini Cove. On June 11, participants take part in a 4Ocean beach cleanup and community dinner. June 12 brings a Paddle Out Rose Ceremony to honor cystic fibrosis warriors, followed by rest and safety checks before the midnight launch. All paddlers must wear Coast Guard-approved personal flotation devices, waterproof whistles, and reflective gear during dark hours, and GPS trackers will be required and active at all times. More information is available at crossingforcysticfibrosis.com and pipersangels.org.

cards.headline: Broadway's 'Beetlejuice' musical plays through June 7 at Kravis Center in West Palm Beach
cards.teaser: The Broadway hit brings its spooky humor and over-the-top visuals to the Alexander W. Dreyfoos Concert Hall with performances through the weekend.
cards.body:
The Broadway musical 'Beetlejuice' opened June 2 at the Kravis Center in West Palm Beach and runs through June 7 at the Alexander W. Dreyfoos Concert Hall. Actor Ryan Stajmiger stars as the mischievous demon made famous in Tim Burton's 1988 film, bringing the character's spooky humor and heartwarming moments to Palm Beach County audiences.

Stajmiger told reporters he has loved the movie since childhood and appreciates that Michael Keaton's iconic performance lasted only 15 minutes of screen time but became unforgettable. The musical follows Lydia Deetz, a strange and unusual teen whose life changes after meeting two recently deceased neighbors and a demon with a flair for trouble. Stajmiger says his favorite part is breaking the fourth wall to communicate directly with the audience, though early in the show's run he experienced an unexpected moment when a wig change went wrong and he performed an entire scene bald.

Performances include 7:30 p.m. shows on June 3 and June 4, 8 p.m. on June 5, matinee and evening performances on June 6, and a closing matinee on June 7. Tickets start at $34.50 and are available directly at kravis.org. The show is recommended for ages 13 and up with parental discretion advised. The Kravis Center continues to draw major Broadway productions, offering Palm Beach County residents big-stage experiences and boosting the region as a cultural destination.

cards.headline: Indian River County grapefruit featured in $2,000 'Jeopardy' question
cards.teaser: Florida citrus got national attention when Indian River County grapefruit was the subject of a high-value question on the game show.
cards.body:
Indian River County grapefruit was featured as a $2,000 question on the game show 'Jeopardy,' bringing national attention to one of the Treasure Coast's signature agricultural products. The appearance highlights the region's long history of citrus production and the reputation Indian River County grapefruit has earned across the country.

Indian River County has been known for decades as a premier grapefruit-growing region, with the fruit's reputation built on the area's ideal growing conditions and careful cultivation practices. The Indian River citrus region actually extends beyond the county's boundaries, encompassing parts of St. Lucie and Martin counties as well.

The 'Jeopardy' appearance provides valuable recognition for local growers who have worked to maintain the quality and reputation of Indian River grapefruit even as Florida's citrus industry has faced challenges from disease and development. The national platform helps reinforce the Treasure Coast's identity as an important agricultural region.

cards.headline: Gifford water tower receives maintenance work in Indian River County
cards.teaser: The Gifford community water tower is getting care and attention as part of infrastructure maintenance in the Indian River County area.
cards.body:
The water tower serving the Gifford community in Indian River County is receiving maintenance work as part of ongoing infrastructure care. The work represents routine upkeep necessary to maintain reliable water service for the unincorporated community located between Vero Beach and Sebastian.

Gifford has a long history as a predominantly African American community in Indian River County, and maintaining essential infrastructure like water towers is critical to ensuring continued quality service for residents. Water towers require regular inspection and maintenance to prevent corrosion, ensure structural integrity, and maintain water pressure throughout the distribution system.

The maintenance work on the Gifford water tower reflects the kind of ongoing infrastructure investment needed in communities throughout the Treasure Coast. Regular care helps extend the life of essential facilities and prevents more costly emergency repairs down the road.

cards.headline: New marina planned for historic downtown waterfront site in Florida city
cards.teaser: A Florida community is moving forward with plans for a new marina on a historic site near its downtown waterfront.
cards.body:
A new marina is planned for a historic site near a downtown waterfront in Florida, though the specific location was not identified in available information. The project represents an investment in waterfront infrastructure and recreational facilities that serve boaters and the broader community.

Marinas provide essential services for recreational and commercial boaters, including docking facilities, fuel, maintenance services, and access to waterways. Developing marina facilities on historic sites requires balancing preservation concerns with modern needs for boating infrastructure.

Waterfront development projects often generate economic activity in downtown areas by attracting boaters who visit local restaurants, shops, and other businesses. The new marina is expected to enhance public access to the waterfront while respecting the historic character of the site.

cards.headline: Sebring Firemen's Festival launches June 3 in Highlands County
cards.teaser: The annual Sebring Firemen's Festival kicks off this week in the Highlands County community south of the Treasure Coast.
cards.body:
The Sebring Firemen's Festival launched June 3 in the Highlands County city located about 80 miles southwest of the Treasure Coast. The annual event brings together community members for entertainment, food, and activities while supporting local firefighters.

Firemen's festivals are traditional community fundraisers that help support volunteer fire departments and emergency services. These events typically feature carnival rides, games, food vendors, and live entertainment, creating family-friendly atmospheres while raising money for essential public safety services.

While Sebring is outside the immediate Treasure Coast region, some residents from Martin, St. Lucie, and Indian River counties may travel to the festival. The event represents the kind of community celebration common in smaller Florida cities where volunteer fire departments play a central role in local life.

hero.headline: Florida Auto Insurance Rates Dropping After 2023 Reforms
hero.body:
Florida drivers are seeing relief at the pump and in their mailboxes as auto insurance rates across the state begin to decline following reforms enacted in 2023. The rate reductions mark a significant shift for Florida motorists who have long paid some of the highest auto insurance premiums in the nation.

The 2023 reforms aimed to address the escalating costs that had made Florida one of the most expensive states for auto insurance coverage. The reforms appear to be achieving their intended goal of making auto insurance more affordable for the state's millions of drivers.

The insurance rate reductions come as Florida continues to grapple with broader economic challenges affecting residents statewide. Auto insurance represents a mandatory expense for the vast majority of Florida households, and any decrease in these costs provides direct financial relief to families across the state. The timing of the rate drops could prove particularly beneficial as many Floridians continue to manage household budgets in the face of other ongoing cost pressures.

The full impact of the 2023 reforms will likely become clearer in the coming months as more insurance companies adjust their rates and additional data becomes available. Florida regulators and legislators will be monitoring the situation to ensure the reforms continue to benefit consumers while maintaining a stable insurance market. The rate decreases represent a policy success for state leaders who championed the 2023 legislation as a necessary step to bring Florida's auto insurance costs more in line with national averages and provide meaningful financial relief to residents across the state.

cards.headline: South Florida Immigration Courts Abruptly Accelerate Hearings
cards.teaser: Immigration courts in South Florida are abruptly moving up hearing dates, creating anxiety among immigrants facing deportation proceedings.
cards.body:
Immigration courts across South Florida have begun abruptly accelerating hearing schedules, leaving many immigrants scrambling to prepare their cases and experiencing significant anxiety about their futures. The sudden change in court timelines has caught immigrants and their legal representatives off guard as cases previously scheduled months or years out are being moved forward with little notice.

The accelerated hearing schedule affects immigrants throughout the South Florida region who are navigating the complex immigration court system. Many of these individuals have been waiting for their day in court while living in the United States, often for extended periods. The sudden compression of timelines creates challenges for both the immigrants themselves and their attorneys, who must now prepare cases on much shorter notice than originally anticipated.

The reasons behind the abrupt acceleration of hearings were not immediately clear, though such changes can stem from administrative directives, staffing changes, or efforts to reduce court backlogs. Immigration courts nationwide have faced significant case backlogs for years, and efforts to speed up proceedings can have major implications for individuals whose futures hang in the balance. The development adds another layer of uncertainty to an already stressful process for immigrants in South Florida communities.

cards.headline: Florida Attorney General Warns Teen Takeover Organizers
cards.teaser: Florida's Attorney General has issued a warning to organizers of teen takeover events, signaling increased state attention to the gatherings.
cards.body:
Florida Attorney General has put organizers of teen takeover events on notice, warning them that they have drawn the attention of the state's top law enforcement office. The warning comes as these large, often disruptive gatherings of young people have become a concern in communities across Florida.

Teen takeover events typically involve large groups of teenagers converging on public spaces, sometimes leading to traffic disruptions, property damage, and public safety concerns. The gatherings have challenged local law enforcement in various Florida cities and prompted calls for stronger responses from state authorities. By issuing this warning, the Attorney General is signaling that the state is prepared to take action against those who organize events that lead to criminal activity or public disorder.

The involvement of the Attorney General's office represents an escalation in the state's response to these events. While local police departments have been the primary responders to teen takeovers in the past, state-level attention suggests potential for broader legal consequences for organizers. The warning serves as both a deterrent to future organizers and a signal to communities that state authorities are taking the issue seriously.

cards.headline: Double Stabbing at USF Off-Campus Housing, Suspect Believed Dead
cards.teaser: Two University of South Florida students were stabbed at an off-campus housing complex, and the suspect is believed to be the person found dead in a separate investigation.
cards.body:
The Hillsborough County Sheriff's Office is investigating a double stabbing at an off-campus student housing complex near the University of South Florida that left two students injured. Authorities believe the suspect in the attack is the same person found dead in a separate investigation on East Fletcher Avenue Wednesday afternoon.

The incident occurred at student housing near the Tampa campus, raising safety concerns for the USF community. The two victims were students at the university who were stabbed in what appears to have been a targeted attack. The condition of the stabbing victims has not been disclosed, but the incident has shaken the off-campus community where many USF students live.

The connection between the stabbing and the body found on East Fletcher Avenue is still under investigation by the Hillsborough County Sheriff's Office. Authorities are working to confirm the identity of the deceased person and establish the full timeline of events. The incident highlights ongoing concerns about student safety in off-campus housing areas near major Florida universities.

cards.headline: University of Florida Presidential Candidate Stuart Bell Addresses Campus Culture
cards.teaser: Stuart Bell, a candidate for University of Florida president, has stated he will not bring back what he termed woke policies to the campus.
cards.body:
Stuart Bell, a hopeful for the University of Florida presidency, has made clear his stance on campus culture by stating he will not bring woke policies back to the institution. The statement comes as the university searches for new leadership and navigates ongoing debates about academic freedom, diversity initiatives, and campus governance.

The University of Florida presidential search is taking place against the backdrop of broader debates about higher education policy in Florida. State leaders have taken an active role in shaping university policies, particularly around issues of diversity, equity, and inclusion programs. Bell's positioning on these cultural issues appears designed to align with the current political climate in Florida higher education.

The selection of UF's next president will have significant implications for one of the state's flagship universities and its tens of thousands of students, faculty, and staff. The presidency of a major research university involves balancing academic priorities, fundraising, state relations, and campus culture. Bell's public statements on campus culture suggest these issues will remain central to discussions about the university's future direction.

cards.headline: Florida Man Sues After Alligator Bites Face
cards.teaser: A Florida man has filed a lawsuit following an incident in which an alligator bit his face.
cards.body:
A Florida man has taken legal action after suffering an alligator bite to his face, filing a lawsuit in connection with the incident. The case highlights the ongoing intersection of human activity and wildlife in Florida, where alligator encounters remain a persistent concern across the state.

Alligator attacks, while relatively rare, do occur in Florida where the reptiles are found in lakes, rivers, canals, and retention ponds throughout the state. When attacks happen, questions often arise about liability, particularly when they occur on managed properties or in areas where the public has been invited. The lawsuit suggests the victim believes someone bears legal responsibility for the circumstances that led to his injuries.

Florida is home to an estimated 1.3 million alligators, and the state's warm climate and abundant waterways create numerous opportunities for human-wildlife interaction. Property owners, managers, and government entities sometimes face legal claims when alligator encounters result in injuries, particularly if adequate warnings were not provided or known alligator populations were not properly managed.

cards.headline: Teen on E-Scooter Hit by Florida Patrol Car After Running Stop Sign
cards.teaser: A Florida Highway Patrol car struck a teenager on an e-scooter who ran a stop sign, an incident captured on video.
cards.body:
A teenager riding an e-scooter was hit by a Florida patrol car after running a stop sign, an incident that was captured on video. The collision raises questions about e-scooter safety and traffic enforcement as these personal mobility devices become increasingly common on Florida roads.

The video shows the teen on the e-scooter failing to stop at a stop sign before entering an intersection where the patrol car was traveling. E-scooters have proliferated in Florida cities in recent years, providing convenient short-distance transportation but also creating new traffic safety challenges. Riders are expected to follow the same traffic laws as other vehicles, including stopping at stop signs and traffic signals.

The incident illustrates the risks associated with e-scooter use, particularly when riders fail to obey traffic laws. While e-scooters offer environmental and practical benefits, they also present safety concerns for both riders and other road users. Florida law enforcement and traffic safety officials continue to grapple with how to regulate and enforce rules around these relatively new forms of transportation.

hero.headline: Martin County Sheriff breaks up multi-county hardware store theft ring in Operation Hammer Time
hero.body:
The Martin County Sheriff's Office announced the arrest of three men involved in a retail theft ring that targeted more than 40 hardware stores across 13 counties between December 2025 and April 2026. Major Ruben Romero identified the suspects as Johnny Batista, 19, Roberto Hernandez-Castro, 39, and Roberto Aldana-Ferrera, 31. The crew stole roughly $500,000 worth of property and caused extensive damage to stores across Martin, Palm Beach and St. Lucie counties, according to Romero.

The suspects hit hardware stores in Stuart, Lake Worth, Delray Beach, Boynton Beach, West Palm Beach, Fort Pierce and Jupiter, as well as stores in Broward County. Investigators say the crews used sledgehammers or other blunt objects to smash glass and often completed the thefts within minutes, before police arrived or alarms were triggered. The stolen goods were taken back to Miami-Dade County, where the suspects lived, to be sold.

Batista was arrested in February for a vehicle theft and remains in Martin County Jail. Aldana-Ferrera is in custody in Georgia, while Hernandez-Castro has a warrant out for his arrest. A fourth suspect, Maikell Fleitas, is deceased. Romero connected Batista to the first known theft at Sewell Hardware in Stuart in December 2025, though investigators believe burglaries happened earlier.

The suspects face charges including racketeering, burglary over $1,000 in damage while masked, burglary of an occupied structure, and burglary of an unoccupied structure. Romero said the thefts have a broader impact on the community. "There's already inflation that we notice severely in our state, and the more they steal, the more damage they cause, the more expensive things are. People can't go to work because they can't afford the tools." Investigators are still looking for one other suspect.

cards.headline: Martin County activists rally at Blake Library to save rare deep-sea coral reef off Fort Pierce
cards.teaser: Dozens of community members gathered at the Blake Library in Martin County after a federally appointed council voted to roll back protections for the Oculina Bank, a rare deep-water coral reef found nowhere else on Earth.
cards.body:
Community members gathered at the Blake Library in Martin County to protest a federal council decision that would roll back longstanding protections for the Oculina Bank, a rare deep-water coral reef located just off the coast of Fort Pierce. Unlike most coral that needs shallow sunlight to survive, the Oculina Bank thrives in deep, dark waters hundreds of feet below the surface and is home to more than 2,000 marine species.

Two proposals would reopen parts of the reef to shrimp trawling, even though scientists say trawling destroyed as much as 90 percent of the reef before federal protections were put in place decades ago. Dr. Grant Gilmore, a scientist who previously dived the reef, told the gathering he is "very concerned about an ecosystem point of view, where your fish don't exist in a vacuum, they need a habitat, they need food. The coral reef was giving them habitat and food. You take that away, you don't have the fish." Mark Perry, executive director of the Florida Oceanographic Society, joined Gilmore in urging the public to help save the reef.

The proposals followed an executive order issued in April 2025 that tasked eight regional councils nationwide to find ways to reinvigorate the fishing industries. Bob Zales, executive director of the Southeastern Fishing Association and a generational shrimper, has said reopening shrimping access to the Oculina Bank is essential for the struggling rock shrimp industry. Council data shows the rock shrimp industry has plummeted from over 700 trips per year in the mid-1990s to under 100 since 2010, with the number of active rock shrimpers dropping from 144 in 1996 to less than 30. A federal agency is preparing a final ruling on the reef's future.

hero.headline: 12 Make-A-Wish children sworn in as junior deputies by St. Lucie County Sheriff
hero.teaser: The St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office honored 12 children from the Make-A-Wish Foundation by swearing them in as junior deputies, including twins where one donated bone marrow to save the other's life.
hero.body:
Twelve children from the Make-A-Wish Foundation were sworn in as junior deputies by St. Lucie County Sheriff Richard Del Toro on Wednesday in what the sheriff called one of the greatest days of his career. The ceremony included tours of the sheriff's office, demonstrations from the SWAT team and K-9 units, and a look at the department's helicopter.

Among the honorees were twins Mia and Daryl Nyack. In 2023, Mia was diagnosed with aplastic anemia, a blood disorder requiring a bone marrow transplant. Her twin brother Daryl donated his bone marrow to save her life, enduring significant pain and spending time in a wheelchair during recovery. Mia said her brother made her feel safe during the frightening experience.

Another junior deputy, Tobias Deleon, was diagnosed with B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia in 2022. His mother Charity said Tobias experienced complications that don't normally happen to children and was even briefly lost before medical staff brought him back. She thanked the sheriff's office for making her son and the other children feel important and welcomed in the community. Sheriff Del Toro said the children left an imprint on his department, telling them they made the sheriff's office's wish come true.

cards.headline: Black bear spotted swimming through Port St. Lucie's Town Park community
cards.teaser: Port St. Lucie police shared rare video footage of a black bear swimming through a waterway in the Town Park neighborhood before running toward nearby homes, prompting wildlife officials to monitor the situation.
cards.body:
Port St. Lucie police released video footage Tuesday showing a black bear swimming through a waterway in the Town Park community before exiting the water and running toward nearby homes. The sighting marks an unusual wildlife encounter along the Treasure Coast, where bear sightings remain rare according to the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission.

The FWC Bear Management Program said they are monitoring the bear and may set a trap to capture and relocate it if the animal doesn't move from the area on its own. Police explained that Florida's black bears become more active this time of year while searching for food, leading to occasional sightings in residential neighborhoods.

Wildlife officials recommend that residents maintain significant distance from any bears they encounter, never approach the animals, and avoid feeding them. Port St. Lucie police advise keeping children and pets away from bears and securing potential food sources including garbage, pet food, and bird seed. If residents encounter a bear, they should remain calm, avoid running, slowly back away while keeping the bear visible, speak in calm firm tones, and ensure the animal has a clear escape route. The Associated Press reported that Florida's black bear population has grown substantially in recent years after decades of conservation efforts, leading to more frequent human-wildlife interactions across the state.

cards.headline: Historic Boston House in Fort Pierce reopens as downtown dining destination
cards.teaser: The Boston House, a Fort Pierce landmark built in 1909 and listed on the National Register of Historic Places, has reopened as a new dining experience aimed at bringing fresh energy to downtown.
cards.body:
The Boston House, located along South Indian River Drive in downtown Fort Pierce, has officially reopened as a dining destination after more than a century serving various roles in the community. Built in 1909 by an engineer for Henry Flagler's Florida East Coast Railway who later became St. Lucie County's third sheriff, the building is listed on the National Register of Historic Places and remains closely tied to the region's early development.

Co-owner Georgette Angelos said the goal is to make guests feel at home automatically while honoring the building's legacy. During renovations, the owners intentionally preserved historic details including low original ceilings and Florida-themed law books that reference the home's past. Angelos described Fort Pierce as eclectic, artistic, and having deep beautiful history, saying the project keeps the authenticity intact while bringing a new breath of fresh air into the town.

General manager Scott Laird said the revival of the property reflects broader momentum in downtown Fort Pierce. He noted that the city has done a great job bringing new life to the downtown area, helping to change Fort Pierce's reputation. Each room in the Boston House offers a distinct experience rooted in local history, blending preservation with a modern dining atmosphere. The reopening represents both a historic landmark's preservation and a renewed gathering place for the community.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie woman sentenced to 3 years in prison for running illegal med spa from backyard shed
cards.teaser: Rosa Mena, 50, of Port St.
cards.body:
Rosa Mena, 50, of Port St. Lucie has been sentenced to three years in prison and five years of probation after operating an unlicensed medical spa out of a shed behind her home on the 5000 block of Northwest Coosa Drive. The case came to light in May 2025 when a victim reported partial facial paralysis after receiving 62 units of Botox injections at Mena's makeshift facility, which she called Miracle Hand and Spa.

The victim, who had been referred by coworkers who previously used Mena's services, paid $325 for the treatment. When the paralysis persisted, the victim asked to see Mena's medical license. Mena provided what turned out to be an altered phlebotomy certificate that had expired in February 2024. Mena also told the victim she was a doctor from the Dominican Republic and offered to reverse the paralysis with vitamin injections, according to Port St. Lucie Police.

A multi-agency investigation involving Port St. Lucie Police, PSL Code Enforcement, the PSL Building Department, PSL Business Tax, and the Florida Department of Health led to a search warrant at Mena's residence. Detectives found medical beds, fat sculpting machines, laser hair removal equipment, laser liposuction machines, and injection devices for fillers and Botox.

Mena was charged with three counts of aggravated battery causing bodily harm, three counts of practicing medicine without an active license, one count of fraud to obtain property worth $300 or more, one count of fraud to obtain property under $20,000, and one count of use of a two-way communication device to facilitate a felony. The case serves as a warning to residents to verify credentials before receiving medical services from unlicensed practitioners.
